sections.title: Welcome to the Rubber-Sheet World
sections.content: Introduce the concept of Topology as 'Rubber-Sheet Geometry.' Explain that unlike Euclidean geometry, topology ignores distances, angles, and areas, focusing instead on the properties of a shape that remain unchanged when it is stretched or twisted.
sections.example: An animation of a flexible rubber square being pulled into a circle, then a triangle, showing they are 'topologically' the same because no tearing occurred.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Continuous Deformation
sections.content: Define the 'rules of the game.' For two shapes to be considered equivalent, you must be able to transform one into the other via continuous deformation. This means stretching, shrinking, and bending are allowed, but tearing holes or gluing parts together is strictly forbidden.
sections.example: Imagine a character named 'Flexi-Cat' made of playdough. Flexi-Cat can stretch his tail to be miles long (allowed), but if he bites his tail to form a loop, he has 'glued' surfaces, which changes his topology.

sections.title: Homeomorphism: The Coffee Mug Paradox
sections.content: Introduce 'Homeomorphism,' the formal term for topological equivalence. If shape A can be morphed into shape B without breaking the rules, they are homeomorphs. This is the core 'equality' sign in topology.
sections.example: The classic 3D animation of a ceramic coffee mug morphing into a doughnut (torus). Because the hole in the handle becomes the hole in the doughnut, they are topologically identical.

sections.title: Topological Invariants: The 'Genus'
sections.content: Explain how mathematicians categorize shapes using 'Invariants'—properties that don't change. The most intuitive invariant is the 'Genus' (the number of holes). Introduce the visual formula: Genus 0 = Sphere, Genus 1 = Torus, Genus 2 = Double Torus.
sections.example: A visual comparison table: A soccer ball (Genus 0), a wedding ring (Genus 1), and a typical shirt button with four holes (Genus 4). No matter how you stretch the ball, it can never become a ring without a 'tear'.

sections.title: Real-World Application: Network Topology
sections.content: Transition from abstract shapes to functional structures. Explain how topology is used in designing subway maps or computer networks where the actual distance between stations doesn't matter as much as 'which station is connected to which.'
sections.example: Compare a geographically accurate map of the London Underground (messy) to the schematic London Tube Map (clean lines). The Tube Map is a 'topological map'—it preserves connectivity while distorting distance for clarity.

sections.title: Summary: The Big Picture
sections.content: Recap the journey from stretching shapes to identifying invariants like the Genus. Emphasize that topology allows us to find deep patterns in complex systems (like DNA or Big Data) by focusing on connections rather than measurements.
sections.example: A final fast-motion montage of various objects (glasses, scissors, keys) being grouped into 'buckets' based on their hole count (Genus).

storyboard.title: Welcome to the Rubber-Sheet World
lecture_lines: Welcome to topology, the study of "rubber-sheet geometry."
Here, we ignore rigid properties like distance and area.
Instead, we focus on shapes that survive continuous stretching.
Watch this square smoothly transform into a circle.
In topology, these shapes are considered exactly the same.
animations: Fade in the text 'TOPOLOGY' in a light blue color (#56B4E9) at the center of the screen.
Transform the text 'TOPOLOGY' into a simple square outline with a blue stroke (#0072B2).
Morph the square outline into a perfect circle outline while maintaining the same blue stroke color (#0072B2).

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: Continuous Deformation
lecture_lines: We follow strict rules called "continuous deformations."
You can stretch, bend, or shrink any shape freely.
However, tearing holes or gluing parts is strictly forbidden.
animations: Display a horizontal yellow line segment (#F0E442) in the center.
Smoothly bend and stretch the yellow line into a complex, winding curve (#F0E442).
Display a red 'X' mark (#D55E00) over a dashed line representing a 'cut' to indicate tearing is forbidden.

storyboard.title: Homeomorphism: The Coffee Mug Paradox
lecture_lines: Mathematicians use the word "homeomorphism" for topological equality.
If shape A can morph into B, they are homeomorphs.
Take this classic example: a coffee mug and a doughnut.
The handle's hole is the only thing that really matters.
To a topologist, they are the same geometric object.
animations: Draw a white 2D outline representing a coffee mug (#FFFFFF) with a distinct handle.
Change the handle's stroke color to orange (#E69F00) to highlight its importance.
Morph the mug outline into a torus (doughnut) shape (#FFFFFF), with the handle becoming the central hole.
Pulse the central hole of the torus with an orange glow (#E69F00) to show its origin.
Display the label 'HOMEOMORPHISM' in bold orange text (#E69F00) above the shape.

storyboard.title: Topological Invariants: The 'Genus'
lecture_lines: We classify shapes using properties that never change, called invariants.
The "genus" counts the number of holes in a surface.
A sphere has genus zero, having no holes at all.
A torus has genus one, like a wedding ring.
You can't turn a sphere into a torus without tearing.
animations: Show a blue sphere (#56B4E9) on the left labeled 'Genus 0' and a green torus (#009E73) in the center labeled 'Genus 1'.
Show a purple double-torus (#CC79A7) on the right labeled 'Genus 2'.
Highlight the holes in each shape (0, 1, and 2 respectively) using a white flash (#FFFFFF).
Morph a 3D-looking cube into the blue sphere to show they are both Genus 0.
Display the summary text 'Genus is an Invariant' in white (#FFFFFF).

storyboard.title: Real-World Application: Network Topology
lecture_lines: Topology helps us navigate complex real-world systems like subways.
Maps prioritize connection paths over geographic accuracy or distance.
This "topological map" makes a messy city easy to understand.
animations: Display a realistic city map with many nodes and messy, curved streets in gray (#999999).
Transform the map into a clean schematic where streets are only horizontal, vertical, or 45-degree angles.
Highlight a specific path between two nodes in bright blue (#0072B2).
Stretch and distort the schematic map while keeping all nodes and path connections unchanged.
Display the text 'CONNECTIVITY IS INVARIANT' in white (#FFFFFF) at the bottom.

storyboard.title: Summary: The Big Picture
lecture_lines: Topology shifts our focus from measurements to structural connections.
We identify deep patterns in DNA, data, and galaxies.
In this flexible world, continuity is the ultimate rule.
animations: Show two labeled 'buckets': 'Genus 0' (blue, #56B4E9) and 'Genus 1' (green, #009E73).
Animate a sphere and a cube moving into the 'Genus 0' bucket (#56B4E9).
Animate a mug and a torus moving into the 'Genus 1' bucket (#009E73).
